name: Dark Neutral Grey
lede: Dark Neutral Grey is a plainly descriptive name: Ridgway's 1912 dictionary uses it for a dark greenish gray, one of the more common named colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A descriptive, not a borrowed, name
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 dictionary lists Dark Neutral Grey at #4C5751, plate LIII, hue 73, tone k, and the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 repeats it in the block it calls "dark greenish gray" [1]. Unlike most names, this one needs no etymology: it describes the swatch directly, and Ridgway's own system records no plant, place or person behind it [1]. The dictionary gives no Munsell notation for this particular swatch [1].

In our color graph the nearest named neighbor is [[traffic-grey-b|Traffic Grey B]], 2.9 units away [1]. A little further, at 4.8 units, is [[pelican|Pelican]] [1]. The swatch sits with our [[grey|grey]] family, its green modifier also pulling it toward [[green|green]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 2.58% of 23,781 paintings, 614 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 293 [2]. That makes it more common than 76% of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 2.9% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 2.2 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Within a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 32% of its 293 appearances [2]. Paul Sérusier is its most devoted painter, holding it in 4 of 26 works here, 5.0 times the baseline of the museums his paintings come from [2]. It is most over-represented in Norway, 3.1 times the expected rate [2]. It shares canvases with [[moss-grey|Moss Grey]] and [[black-grey|Black Grey]] more often than chance, at 3.3 and 2.9 times the expected rate [2]. The earliest match dates to 1099, 813 years before Ridgway recorded the name, a floor rather than a first [2].
